opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, that was one of the hardest parts of the whole project, because internal numbers can fool you. When you train a system against itself, or against earlier versions of itself, you can see the Elo going up and up, but you never really know whether you're climbing a real hill or just getting very good at exploiting your own blind spots.

So we thought about it in layers. First, we tested against the strongest existing Go programs at the time, things like Crazy Stone and Zen, which were the commercial state of the art. AlphaGo was beating them almost all the time, even when we gave them handicap stones. That told us we were clearly ahead of every other computer program, but it didn't tell us much about humans, because those programs were still only at a strong amateur level.

The next step was playing a real professional. That's why we invited Fan Hui, the European champion, to play a formal match. I remember we were nervous, because a professional plays very differently from a program. They probe for weaknesses, they play strange moves to see how you react. When AlphaGo won that match five to nothing, that was the first moment we thought, okay, this is real.

But even then, Fan Hui was a two-dan professional, and Lee Sedol was in a completely different league. So between those matches we kept improving the system and kept evaluating it internally, and we tried to be very paranoid about it. We'd look at games where it lost against its own earlier versions, look for systematic failure modes, and we had strong Go players, including Fan Hui himself after he joined us as an advisor, looking at its games and trying to find holes.

In the end, though, the only way to know for sure was to play the match. You can build as much confidence as you want internally, but you have to put it in front of the best player in the world, in public, and accept that it might fail. And as we saw in game four, it did have weaknesses we hadn't fully found. That was actually a very valuable lesson for us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AlphaGo’s blind spots and weaknesses, but does not compare its failures to language-model hallucinations.

r002.rationale: It says the only way to know for sure was to play the world’s best player, and that the match exposed weaknesses the team had not found.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is that for a long time we couldn't know, and that was the uncomfortable part. Internally, the only thing you have is self-play and matches against previous versions of your own system. You can see the Elo going up, you can see version N beating version N-minus-one, but that's a closed world. The system could be very good at beating itself and still have blind spots that a strong human would find immediately. We'd seen that with earlier Go programs, and we were quite paranoid about it.

So the first real test was playing against existing programs, things like Crazy Stone and Zen, the strongest Monte Carlo tree search engines at the time. AlphaGo was winning almost every game, including with handicap stones, and that told us we were well beyond the previous state of the art. But those programs were still amateur level, so it didn't answer the question we actually cared about, which was whether we were at a professional level.

That's really why the Fan Hui match mattered so much. Fan Hui was the European champion, a professional 2-dan, and playing him was the first time the system faced someone who had spent his whole life playing Go at a serious level. And we did it properly, formal games, full time controls, with him coming to our office. We won five to zero in the formal games, which was a big moment, but I'd say the informal games were almost more informative, because he did win some of those, and you could see where the weaknesses were.

The other thing Fan Hui gave us was not just a result but understanding. He stayed on and worked with us, played the system constantly, and he could tell us in human terms what it was doing wrong. He'd say this move looks fine but a professional would never play it, and that kind of feedback is something you simply cannot get from a win-rate curve.

And then of course the Lee Sedol match was a different thing entirely. Between Fan Hui and Seoul there was a huge gap in strength, and we spent those months trying to close it, with much more training, a lot more self-play, and a much better value network. By the time we went to Korea, our internal estimates said we should be competitive, but I'll be honest, nobody really knew. The estimates were extrapolations, and the whole point of playing the best player in the world is that there's no extrapolation left to hide behind. Game four, where Lee Sedol found that wedge move and the system fell apart, showed us exactly why the uncertainty was justified. The system had a genuine weakness, and only a human of his level was going to find it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AlphaGo’s blind spots and failures, but does not compare them to language-model hallucinations.

r002.rationale: The response says professional human matches exposed weaknesses and that only a human at Lee Sedol’s level was likely to find the weakness shown in game four.

astra-6.text: We needed to test it against strong human players. Playing against other programs, or looking at how well it did in self-play, could tell us that we were making progress, but it didn’t necessarily tell us where we stood relative to the best people. So the idea was to arrange a proper match, under conditions where the result would be meaningful. And you have to be willing to discover that your system isn’t as strong as you thought—that’s part of why you do the test.
